genxml.title: REX1 raster engine on the Indigo Entry graphics board (LG1)
genxml.doc: Register file of the REX1 chip as the Indigo's Entry graphics board presents it on the GIO graphics slot. Offsets are bytes from the board base (0x1f3f0000 for the first head, 0x1f3f8000 for a second). Every register is 32 bits wide. A register written at its offset is only stored (the SET alias). The same register at offset + 0x800 (the GO alias) is stored and then the latched command is executed. Names are the ones the shipped diagnostics (ide) print for the REX register test, where it prints one; the rest use the names of the NetBSD sgimips light driver. The three off-chip ports (WCLOCK, RWDAC, RWVC1) are covered here as REX registers; the chips behind them are in devices/vc1 and devices/bt479. Grades follow AGENTS.md: established means the whole routine was read in the shipped Indigo kernel graphics driver or the Indigo PROM; inferred is a reading with the reasoning given; unknown means no shipped software settles it. Nothing was measured on a board.

struct.name: COMMAND
struct.doc: Drawing command. Bits 31:28 hold the logic operation, the low bits the opcode and flags listed as CMD_ constants. A write at 0x000 stores it; a write at 0x800 (or a read of 0x800) executes the command that is now latched, using the coordinate and colour registers as they stand. The PROM's probe writes 0 here and reads 0x800 (a no-op); the kernel's glyph path writes the command, then writes ZPATTERN at its GO alias once per row. A qtest can discriminate: a command written at 0x000 draws nothing, the same word at 0x800 draws, and a read of 0x800 draws what the latched command says. Bits 27:20 of values the kernel and PROM write are zero except bit 23 and bit 24 (ZOPAQUE, ZCONTINUE: not set by shipped code) and bit 21 (all three) and bit 16 (second only) in the pixel-memory probe commands 0x30200021, 0x30210021 and 0x30200023 that lightInitInfo and the PROM board-info routine use (see the CMD_PIXMEM constants and rwaux1). Bit 21 is inferred to be host data through RWAUX1, bit 1 of the last to be a read opcode, and bit 16 is unknown. The direction a pattern or block draw steps y is toward YENDI (inferred from the PROM glyphs, which end at YENDI 0, and NetBSD glyphs, which end below YSTARTI), not a fixed down.

struct.name: AUX1
struct.doc: Auxiliary control word, one per window context. initRex zeroes it. lightAux1Register builds a value from a window's saved value with bits 4:2 cleared, sets bit 4 when the request word's second field is 1, bit 2 when bit 0 of its third field is set and bit 3 when bit 1 is set, then stores it here (only for the window that owns the screen) or in the window's saved context. The shipped header names the bits FRACTION0 and FRACTION1 (0, 1), DBLDST0 and DBLDST1 (2, 3), DBLSRC (4), DOUBLEBUF (5), COLORCOMPLT, COLORCOMPEQ and COLORCOMPGT (6, 7, 8) and DITHERRANGE (9); the roles are inferred from the names: bits 2 and 3 pick which buffer a draw writes, bit 4 which one it reads, bit 5 turns double buffering on. The X server's four-pixel tile fill and PutImage store 0x28 or 0x2c (DOUBLEBUF with DBLDST1, and DBLDST0 for 0x2c) and its GetImage 0x30 (DOUBLEBUF with DBLSRC). The pixel-memory probe stores 0x100 (COLORCOMPGT) here before its second write. Software expects only bits 9:0 (a software expectation; ten bits is inferred as the hardware width): both the ide register test and the 4.0.5G PROM power-on test write a 32-bit pattern and require the read-back to equal the pattern masked to 0x3ff (0x155 for 0x55555555, 0x2aa for 0xaaaaaaaa), so a store keeps ten bits and a read returns them. A model run that returned the whole word made the PROM print 'Graphics diagnostic FAILED' on the Entry; that comes from a trace of our own model, not from a board. A qtest can write 0x55555555 at 0x004 and read 0x155. The IRIS GL library's context set-up stores 2 (FRACTION1 alone). GL contexts use 0x202 (single-buffered, FRACTION1 and DITHERRANGE) or 0x222 plus buffer bits: GL_FRONT is DBLDST0 (0x226), GL_BACK DBLDST1 and DBLSRC (0x23a), both 0x22e, the pair exchanged after each swap. devices/rex1/gl-context-state.md.

struct.name: XSTATE
struct.doc: Packed draw state word. The kernel stores 0x03ff0000 here before each full-screen clear (rexClear, the command word 0x329 with no logic-operation nibble), and the X server (X server driver functions rexInitHW, rexDrawSolidRects, rexDrawPoints, rexDrawImage, rexCopyRect, rexImageGlyphBltTE8) stores it before nearly every draw. The X server builds it as colour index in bits 7:0, plane write mask in bits 23:16 and the X raster-operation code in bits 27:24 (GXcopy is 3, so the clear value 0x03ff0000 is: replace, all eight planes, colour 0; the copy path ORs 0x20 into the top byte). Those field roles are inferred from what the writers pack, not from a manual. The operation is a value from 0 to 15 shifted left by 24, so it occupies bits 27:24; bit 29 is a separate flag that only the copy words set (0x20000000 in rexCopyRect, 0x23ff0000 in rexValidateWindowPriv), role unknown. Open and settled only as a model constraint: the X server fills with command 0x329 and the colour from here, while the kernel's per-rectangle fill (light_sboxfi) uses 0x30000329 and the colour from COLORREDI (the kernel's rexClear does write XSTATE); rexImageGlyphBltTE8 fills its background with 0x30000329 after writing only XSTATE and loads COLORREDI afterwards, which is the discriminating case for the shared reading. The one reading that satisfies every shipped writer is that XSTATE bits 7:0 and COLORREDI are the same eight bits of state. The shipped header names bits 31:28 XSTATE_ZOPAQUE, XSTATE_LSOPAQUE, XSTATE_LOGICSRC and XSTATE_COLORAUX, the same names as command bits 23, 22, 19 and 21, so the upper nibble is the X server's way of keeping those command flags as state (inferred); the tile fill sets bit 28 and the copy words set bit 29. The ide test writes all 32 bits and expects them back unmasked.

struct.name: XSTARTI
struct.doc: Draw start x as an integer. Twelve bits are kept (the ide test mask is 0xfff) and appear in XSTART at bit 15 and above: lightProbe writes 0x12345678 here and expects 0x033c0000 from XSTART. A qtest can discriminate: write 0x12345678, read XSTART at 0x14, expect 0x033c0000; whether XSTARTI itself reads back is unknown: no shipped code and not the ide test (which reads XSTART) reads offset 0xc. The ide test confirms the derivation: write at 0xc, read at 0x14, expect (value & 0xfff) << 15.

struct.name: XSTARTF
struct.doc: Draw start x, fraction. Test mask 0x7fffff. Offset read from the ide test. Software that draws only rectangles never writes it. Offset established by the ide test. A write here appears in XSTART bits 26:4 (the ide test reads 0x14, not 0x10). 'F' is the ide name; the readback shows the register feeds XSTART bits 26:4 (inferred as a write alias of XSTART).

struct.name: XSTART
struct.doc: Draw start x, integer and fraction combined: 27 bits in the ide test mask, integer in bits 26:15. Read at offset 0x14 by the board probe after XSTARTI was written; the value read is the probe presence test (PROBE_READBACK). lightPcxSwap reads it back and later stores the saved value at 0x14 itself, so a store here must be kept whole (the same holds for YSTART at 0x24, COLORRED/GREEN/BLUE at 0x3c/0x44/0x4c and the slope registers at 0x50 to 0x58): a model that derives XSTART only from XSTARTI loses a context restore. Whether a write here also reflects in XSTARTI: unknown.

struct.name: XENDF
struct.doc: Draw end x, fraction (ide mask 0x7ff800). Offset established by the ide test. Holds the end x with the integer in bits 22:11 (a write to XENDI at 0x84 reads back here as value & 0xfff shifted left 11; written directly, only bits 22:11 stick). Not a fraction field as the name suggests.

struct.name: YSTARTI
struct.doc: Draw start y as an integer, 12 bits kept; the ide test writes it and reads YSTART (0x24) expecting (value & 0xfff) << 15. Software stores 767 minus its own y, which counts up from the bottom, so the stored value is the display row counted from the top of the 768-line screen (inferred: the PROM console prints its first text row at the largest console y, and NetBSD stores unflipped row numbers). See the Y origin section of the REX1 page.

struct.name: YSTARTF
struct.doc: Draw start y, fraction. Offset established by the ide test. Mirror of XSTARTF for y; a write appears in YSTART bits 26:4. For lines the IRIX 6.2 GL writes the float 4096.0 + y at the centre of the first pixel, so the mantissa is the 12.11 start; the ide read-back shows YSTART = mantissa << 4 (12.15). devices/rex1/true-lines.md.

struct.name: YSTART
struct.doc: Draw start y, integer and fraction combined, counterpart of XSTART. Offset inferred; no shipped code reads it. Offset established by the ide test. Combined y start, integer in bits 26:15 (the same derivation the probe uses for XSTART).

struct.name: YENDF
struct.doc: Draw end y, fraction. Offset established by the ide test. Holds the end y with the integer in bits 22:11, as XENDF.

struct.name: XSAVE
struct.doc: Saved x start (the x that a block-draw returns to at the start of each row, inferred from its name and the context save). lightPcxSwap saves it with the other window registers. Offset established by the ide test. Twelve bits kept. No routine of the IRIX 6.2 GL that draws lines, triangle rows, spans, points, clears or copies stores it. devices/rex1/true-lines.md.

struct.name: MINORSLOPE
struct.doc: Line-draw minor-axis slope. Never written by the shipped light code for rectangles, text or points. Only the name (ide) and the slot between XSAVE and XYMOVE support it. Offset established by the ide test. Written and read back unmasked. Sign rule, from the ide REX test: 17 bits are kept, bit 31 is the sign, bit 16 of a negative magnitude is ignored and the result is the 17-bit two's complement. The GL writes 256.0 + m or -256.0 + m (0x43800000 plus the fraction), which gives 15 fraction bits; each step along the major axis adds it to the minor coordinate. devices/rex1/true-lines.md.

struct.name: XYMOVE
struct.doc: Copy source offset: x delta in the high 16 bits and y delta in the low 16, each source minus destination, in stored coordinates (display row = stored y). The X server (X server driver function rexCopyRect) computes dx as source x minus destination x0 and dy as source y minus destination y0, masks dy to 16 bits and stores (dx << 16) | dy at the GO alias (0x834) after the rectangle and the copy command 0x80329 are set up; it chooses XSTARTI..XENDI ascending when dx is not negative and descending when it is, and YSTARTI..YENDI ascending when dy is not negative and descending when it is, so the engine must honour either order of the two registers. That fixes the sign for the X server and agrees with NetBSD. The only remaining doubt is the PROM copy routine, whose callers were not found. For a destination x0 below 4 and dx negative the X server also stores XYWIN 0x07fc0800 around the copy (see XYWIN). The ide mask 0x7ff07ff shows eleven bits kept per half. A qtest can discriminate: write 0x00100005 at 0x34 and 0x80329 or 0x30080329 at 0, then a copy from (x+16, y+5) happens when 0x800 is touched, and a rectangle with YSTARTI greater than YENDI copies bottom row first. The IRIX 6.2 GL's rectangle copy stores the same layout with the word 0x30280329.

struct.name: COLORREDI
struct.doc: Foreground pixel colour (the ide test reads a write back through COLORRED at 0x3c as (value & 0xff) << 11), an 8-bit index into the colour map (the board has 8 bits per pixel). The kernel's colour routine stores the index at this offset after the busy bit clears; the PROM's colour routine does too. The ide test calls the register COLORREDI with an 8-bit mask; RED because the chip's colour path starts with red.

struct.name: COLORRED
struct.doc: Red channel with fraction for shaded draws, 20 bits in the ide mask. Offset by name order. Offset established by the ide test. COLORRED holds the red channel with its integer part (COLORREDI, 8 bits) in bits 18:11. Shaded draws: the IRIX 6.2 GL stores the float c + 6144.0, so the word is 0x45c00000 + c * 2048 (bits above 19 are ignored by the chip, 9 integer and 11 fraction bits are kept) and a negative c wraps modulo 512. Whether the chip clamps or wraps out-of-range colours is unknown. devices/rex1/shaded-drawing.md.

struct.name: COLORGREENI
struct.doc: Green channel integer (shaded draws). Never written by shipped light code. Offset from the ide name order and NetBSD. Offset established by the ide test. A write here appears in COLORGREEN bits 18:11.

struct.name: COLORGREEN
struct.doc: Green channel with fraction. Offset established by the ide test. 20 bits kept. Same format as COLORRED.

struct.name: COLORBLUEI
struct.doc: Blue channel integer. Offset established by the ide test. A write here appears in COLORBLUE bits 18:11.

struct.name: COLORBLUE
struct.doc: Blue channel with fraction. Offset established by the ide test. 20 bits kept. Same format as COLORRED. A store at the GO alias (0x84c) runs the latched command: the GL's flat RGB lines and clears end that way.

struct.name: SLOPERED
struct.doc: Red slope for shaded lines and spans. Not written by shipped light code. Offset established by the ide test. Slope registers are signed: the ide test expects bit 19 of the stored value to read back also in bit 20. Sign rule, from the ide REX register test: bit 31 is the sign and bits 19:0 the magnitude; with bit 31 set the stored value is the 21-bit two's complement of the magnitude (bit 20 of the written value is cleared first), read back with bit 20 ORed with bit 19; bits 30:21 of a write are ignored. The GL writes m + 6144.0 for a positive slope and m - 6144.0 for a negative one. devices/rex1/shaded-drawing.md.

struct.name: SLOPEGREEN
struct.doc: Green slope. Not written by shipped light code. NetBSD names offset 0x54 of the configuration page WCLOCKREV, which is a different page. Offset established by the ide test. As SLOPERED. Same rule as SLOPERED.

struct.name: SLOPEBLUE
struct.doc: Blue slope. Not written by shipped light code. Offset established by the ide test. As SLOPERED. Same rule as SLOPERED. A store at the GO alias (0x858) runs the latched command: the GL's smooth RGB lines end that way.

struct.name: COLORBACK
struct.doc: Background colour index used for pattern zeros when ZOPAQUE is set. The shipped kernel and PROM glyph paths never write it (transparent background); NetBSD does. Offset established by the ide test. Eight bits kept.

struct.name: ZPATTERN
struct.doc: Pixel pattern for the pattern-enabled commands. Software writes it at the GO alias (0x860): each write draws one row of the glyph, taking pattern bits 31 downward, the row's bits shifted into the top half for 16-wide glyphs (the kernel shifts each halfword left by 16) and into bit 24 for 8-wide (NetBSD). With STOPONX, XYCONTINUE and BLOCK, y steps by one row after each write. A qtest can discriminate: set XSTARTI, XENDI, YSTARTI, write command 0x300005b9 at 0 and 0x80000000 at 0x860, and exactly one pixel at the start column is drawn.

struct.name: LSPATTERN
struct.doc: Line stipple pattern. Not written by shipped light code. Offset established by the ide test. Fully read/write. The IRIX 6.2 GL stores the 16-bit GL stipple bit-reversed into both halves; the X server stores a pattern word rotated left by the distance already covered, then a no-op GO store of COMMAND. The first pixel drawn takes bit 31 (inferred from the GL reversal of OpenGL bit-0-first, the X server rotation and the ZPATTERN order). devices/rex1/true-lines.md.

struct.name: LSMODE
struct.doc: Line stipple mode. Not written by shipped light code. NetBSD's configuration-page name CFGMODE for offset 0x68 is a different page. Offset established by the ide test. 20 bits kept. The IRIX 6.2 GL line stipple writes 0xf0000 | n << 8 | n: length field 15 in 19:16 (a 32-bit pattern, as the X server's (width - 17) << 16) and n in 15:8 and 7:0, where n is the GL repeat factor 1 to 256 masked to 8 bits (256 is stored as 0; no subtraction of one).

struct.name: AWEIGHT
struct.doc: Antialias weight. Not written by shipped light code. Offset established by the ide test. Fully read/write. The IRIX 6.2 GL writes 0xdb987642 once at context set-up (the IRIS GL library holds the same constant) and nothing in it reads or rewrites the register; the GL antialiases lines in software. No dither role is evidenced, and no shipped software varies it or issues the antialias opcodes with it (the IRIS GL library writes the same constant at set-up). Its eight nibbles fall steadily (13, 11, 9, 8, 7, 6, 4, 2). devices/rex1/shaded-drawing.md.

struct.name: RWAUX1
struct.doc: Read/write auxiliary word used to read and write pixel memory with a draw command. lightInitInfo writes 0x01081020 here, then 0x09090909 with a 0x30210021 command, runs 0x30200023 and compares the result word read back at 0x870 with 0x01080909 or 0x09091020 to record a 0, 1 or 0xff in byte 0x29 of the board info it hands to GfxRegisterBoard. Data flow (inferred from the constants): the first write puts the four bytes 01 08 10 20 into pixels 0 to 3 of stored row 0, the second replaces exactly one pair of them with 09 (outcome 0 = pixels 2 and 3 replaced, outcome 1 = pixels 0 and 1 replaced, if the high byte is pixel 0), and the read returns the four pixels. All three commands are executed through RWAUX1's GO alias, so RWAUX1 is the data port of the probe. What each outcome means for the board (pixel memory arrangement): unknown; no object read uses info byte 0x29 afterwards. The PROM runs the probe unconditionally; the kernel runs it only when CONFIGMODE bits 7:4 read 0. A qtest can discriminate only by replaying that sequence, which needs the draw unit to move words between RWAUX1 and the frame buffer; any model that yields 0x01080909 or 0x09091020 satisfies every shipped reader, and a choice between them is an approximation.

struct.name: RWAUX2
struct.doc: Second read/write auxiliary word. Not written by shipped light code. Offset established by the ide test. Fully read/write.

struct.name: RWMASK
struct.doc: Plane write mask for read/write pixel access. lightInitInfo and the PROM write 0xff (all eight planes) before the pixel-memory probe. The ide mask 0xffff shows sixteen bits kept, and the ide graphics shell's write-mask command stores its argument here, so the low byte is the pixel write mask (the shipped header's comment calls the register readmask and writemask, in that order, without saying which half is which). The kernel's board-info routine writes it only when CONFIGMODE bits 7:4 read 0; the PROM writes it unconditionally. The X server never writes RWMASK: it keeps the write mask in XSTATE bits 23:16, but it is not the 0xff the board-info routine left: lightPcxSwap saves RWMASK into, and restores it from, the rendering node's image, a node made by lightCreateDDRN has a zero image, and the first load of a never-saved node writes 0 (platforms/lg1/colormap-install.md). The shipped desktop draws with RWMASK 0 and would be blank if hardware gated RWAUX1 host-data writes or reads (tile fill, PutImage, GetImage) with it, so it is inferred not to. The X server's lines, dashes and glyphs also draw with a non-zero logic-operation nibble and RWMASK 0, taking the plane mask from XSTATE 23:16, so the nibble does not decide either. The IRIX 6.2 GL stores 0xff at context set-up, then after every draw-buffer change the window's full mask (0xf for the 4-bit window, 3 for the overlay, 0xff for the 8-bit one) or 0 when the GL draw buffer is none, and no other value, and never stores XSTATE. The hardware rule for how RWMASK and XSTATE 23:16 combine is unknown; every shipped writer is satisfied by their OR. devices/rex1/gl-context-state.md.

struct.name: SMASK1X
struct.doc: Screen mask 1, x range: maximum x in bits 25:16 and minimum x in bits 9:0, each clipped to 0..1023 (the object clamps with 0x3ff). Software computes the window's visible rectangle clipped to the screen and writes it here when window 1 is the active one.

struct.name: SMASK1Y
struct.doc: Screen mask 1, y range, same packing, clipped to 0..767 (0x2ff). The y values are flipped (height minus row minus one) before packing, so they use the same stored-y convention as the drawing registers: row counted from the top of the screen (see the Y origin section of the REX1 page).

struct.name: XENDI
struct.doc: Draw end x (integer, inclusive): the last column a STOPONX command draws. The ide test reads it back through XENDF (0x18) as (value & 0xfff) << 11.

struct.name: YENDI
struct.doc: Draw end y (integer, inclusive), top-down row like YSTARTI. The glyph commands also use the order of YSTARTI and YENDI to pick the direction rows advance: toward YENDI. The ide test reads it back through YENDF (0x28) as (value & 0xfff) << 11. light_sboxfi and the PROM fill store 767 minus the top row here and 767 minus the bottom row in YSTARTI, so YSTARTI <= YENDI.

struct.name: SMASK2X
struct.doc: First of six consecutive screen-mask words, in the order SMASK2X, SMASK2Y, SMASK3X, SMASK3Y, SMASK4X, SMASK4Y. The six-word run is established by the context save and the name-to-word assignment by the ide test's offsets. Packing as smask1x. Offset established by the ide test. The six names map to the six consecutive words in this order.

struct.name: SMASK2Y
struct.doc: Screen mask word 2Y. Packing as smask1x. Added in the 2026-11-23 review so the generated header names all six.

struct.name: SMASK3X
struct.doc: Screen mask word 3X. Packing as smask1x. Added in the 2026-11-23 review so the generated header names all six.

struct.name: SMASK3Y
struct.doc: Screen mask word 3Y. Packing as smask1x. Added in the 2026-11-23 review so the generated header names all six.

struct.name: SMASK4X
struct.doc: Screen mask word 4X. Packing as smask1x. Added in the 2026-11-23 review so the generated header names all six.

struct.name: SMASK4Y
struct.doc: Screen mask word 4Y. Packing as smask1x. Added in the 2026-11-23 review so the generated header names all six.

struct.name: AUX2
struct.doc: Second auxiliary control word. Both initialisations store 0x20000000. lightSetDestinationPlanes keeps bits 28:0 of the window's saved value, ORs in the request's top three bits and, for the window on screen, waits for the engine to go idle and stores the result here, so the top three bits select which plane group a draw reaches. The shipped header names them as one three-bit code, not as three flags: NOPLANES 0, PIXELPLANES 1, OVERLAYPLANES 2 and CIDPLANES 3 (shifted left 29). The X server's plane-group writes agree: 0x20000000 for the displayed pixel planes, 0x40000000 for the overlay clear and 0x60000000 for the window-id fill, whose value is limited to 0 to 3 (rexDrawCID) like the ide CID memory test. The ide mask 0x7fffffff shows 31 bits kept. The X server's line, point and span batches (rexLineSS, rexSegmentSS, rexPolyPoint, rexSolidFillSpans) store (group << 29) | 0xf11 at the start and plain group << 29 at the end, so the low twelve bits are used and the value 0xf11 is not a command word. The header names bits 3:0 SMASK0 to SMASK3 (screen mask enables), bits 7:4 their inside/outside polarity and bits 23:8 four CID match nibbles, so 0xf11 reads as screen mask 0 enabled, inside polarity and CID match nibble 1 set to 0xf (inferred from the names; no shipped code states the effect). The X server's clip table for rendering-node windows (rexValidateClip, 6.2 data 0x5e573830) enables one more screen mask per visible rectangle, up to three (table in devices/rex1/gl-context-state.md; inside polarity everywhere, one 0xf CID nibble per enabled mask); the kernel's lightValidateClip builds 0xf1 | (1 << cid) << 8 for CID-clipped windows; for four to ten visible rectangles rexValidateClip sends the table entry for the obscured-rectangle count ANDed with 0x00ffff1f, clearing polarity bits 7:5, so the enabled masks 1 to 3 have the clear polarity (read as outside, a software expectation from that use and the header names). GL and kernel window contexts use 0xff1 in the low twelve bits (the X server's batches 0xf11): by the header's names screen mask enable bit 0 (the first pair, SMASK1X and SMASK1Y) with inside polarity bit 4, polarity bits 7:5 set on disabled masks, CID match nibble 1 = 0xf. devices/rex1/gl-context-state.md.

struct.name: DIAGVRAM
struct.doc: VRAM diagnostic access. No shipped kernel or PROM runtime path touches it; the ide VRAM test is the only candidate user and was not read. Offset and role: unknown.

struct.name: WCLOCK
struct.doc: Port to the pixel clock generator and the board configuration byte; the byte is picked by CFGSEL. Reading with CFGSEL 4 (after a dummy read of the GO alias and a one microsecond wait) returns: bits 2:0 board revision, bits 5:3 monitor type, bit 6 set when no video board is present. light_init stores them in bytes 0x28, 0x2b and 0x2c of the board info. Writing with CFGSEL 2 clocks the clock generator's program bytes in: initClock writes 17 bytes in a row to the SET and GO aliases, selected by board revision (below 2: the first of the two 17-byte clock tables in the driver, 2 and above: the second). A qtest can discriminate: CFGSEL 4 then a read of GO and SET returns the configured byte; a model needs a settable board revision to take the revision 1 path (the PROM and kernel need the revision below 2 branch for the Bt479 colour map).

struct.name: RWDAC
struct.doc: Port to the colour map chip. CFGSEL picks the chip register (see CFGSEL constants). Software writes the same byte to RWDAC and to its GO alias; the second write is what performs the transfer. A read of its GO alias returns the chip register value. light_read_bt_colormaps and light_read_lut_colormaps issue one GO read, discard it, and then read the GO alias 768 times per bank (bulk reads: the same one-deep pipeline as RWVC1 fits). The X server reads the command register back (CONFIGSEL 6: GO read, then RWDAC read) for read-modify-write of the blank bit (X server driver function rexBlankScreen) and in rexDisplayCursor, so the DAC command register must be readable. Whether the SET read after a GO read adds anything beyond the pipeline: unknown.

struct.name: CONFIGSEL
struct.doc: Three-bit function selector shared by WCLOCK, RWDAC and RWVC1: the value written here is the chip register index the next access to any of the three ports addresses. Values 0 to 6 are used (CFGSEL constants); 7 is not written by shipped code. Readback returns the written value (lightPositionCursor saves and later restores it by reading it back). A qtest can discriminate: write 5, read back 5; write 8, read back 0 (the 0x7 mask, from the ide test).

struct.name: RWVC1
struct.doc: Port to the video controller (VC1), same SET/GO scheme as RWDAC with its GO alias 0x800 above it. A write stores the byte at SET and again at GO; a GO store alone also works (lightSetDisplayMode stores only the GO alias). Reads: every reader does GO read then SET read for a single byte, and the bulk readers (light_read_displaymodes, light_read_scan) issue one GO read whose value they discard and then read only the GO alias, once per byte. Both fit a one-deep read pipeline: a GO read returns the byte fetched by the previous GO read and starts the fetch of the next, and a SET read returns the byte the last GO read fetched; a model where a GO read returns and consumes the current byte makes every bulk reader skip its first byte. The kernel retrace handler and lightPositionCursor read the VC1 address counter back through CONFIGSEL 4 (low) and 5 (high) while a user process may be in the middle of a data transfer; see devices/vc1. The VC1 internal register file behind CFGSEL is in devices/vc1.

struct.name: TOGGLECTXT
struct.doc: Written with 0 in the middle of a window context swap. lightPcxSwap reads ten registers (XSTART, YSTART, COLORRED, COLORGREEN, COLORBLUE, LSPATTERN, LSMODE, ZPATTERN, XSAVE, RWAUX1), stores 0 here, then reads about twenty-four more (XSTART, YSTART, the colour and slope registers, XENDF, YENDF, AUX1, the pattern registers, XSAVE, MINORSLOPE, XYMOVE, COLORBACK, AWEIGHT, RWAUX1, RWAUX2, RWMASK, COMMAND, SMASK1X, SMASK1Y); the load side mirrors it. Inferred from the repeated registers (XSTART, COLORRED and others appear in both passes): the engine holds two copies of part of the drawing state and a write here switches which one the register offsets address. A flat model that keeps one copy and ignores the write returns the same values in both passes and restores consistently. Whether a read is defined: unknown.

struct.name: CONFIGMODE
struct.doc: Configuration and status. Bit 0 is the engine busy flag: all software spins until it is clear before touching a drawing register (the kernel and the PROM do it in every drawing routine). Bits 28:24 (mask 0x1f000000) must also be zero before a VC1 access in lightPositionCursor and the retrace handler: inferred to be a count of commands still queued in the FIFO, which the busy bit alone does not cover. The X server polls a second count, bits 12:8 (five bits): before a burst of register stores it waits until that field is at most 21 minus its gfifo level setting, 14 at the default level 7 (rexLineSS, rexPolyPoint, rexZeroPolyArc, rexImageGlyphBltTE8; fixed limits of 5 and 8 appear in rexSolidFillSpans), so the 5-bit field is inferred to be the graphics FIFO fill level, with the level setting the number of stores the X server allows per primitive. Bits 7:4 are read by lightInitInfo (value 0 triggers the pixel-memory probe described under rwaux1, any other value plus one is stored as a board option byte). initRex and the pixel DMA path store 0x807fe000. The X server (driver function rexInitHW) stores 0x80000000 | 0x40000000 | 0x00180000 | (level << 13) with level 7 by default (see the CPU-board ranges below, or the number in the environment variable REX_GFIFO_LEVEL), raises the level field to 31 for glyph and arc runs (0xc01be000) and writes 0x80000000 | 0x00180000 | (level << 13), without bit 30, only around the pixel DMA of a large PutImage (the CPU-store PutImage path leaves bit 30 set); so bits 17:13 are inferred to be a FIFO-level threshold (the interrupt on GIO line 0 or the stall point), bits 20:19 are constant 11 in every X server store, and bit 30 is set except while the pixel DMA feeds RWAUX1 (role unknown). The default level of 7 becomes 9 or 11 only when an inventory value in the CPU-board range is read at start (0x400 to 0x43f: 9, or 11 with the board-info flags bit 6 set; 0x440 to 0x1fff: 7, or 9 with bit 6 set). lightPcxSwap saves the word xor 0x80000000 and restores it unchanged, so bit 31 is read inverted of what was written. Role of bit 31 and of bits 22:21: unknown. A qtest can discriminate: bit 0 reads 1 while a command is executing and 0 after; the PROM 300000 microsecond polling loop in lightProbe (done when bit 0 clears) must not time out; a model with synchronous drawing may return 0 in bits 28:24 and 12:8 and satisfy every shipped reader.

struct.name: XYWIN
struct.doc: Window origin offset: x in bits 27:16 and y in bits 11:0, 0x800 each at init (the window offset of 2048 that centres a 12-bit coordinate space; the centring is inferred). NetBSD match accepts a board whose XYWIN reads 0x08000800. The X server stores 0x08000800 in rexInitHW and, for a right-to-left copy or a PutImage that starts below x = 4, temporarily stores 0x07fc0800 (x origin 4 lower) and loads XSTARTI and XENDI 4 higher, then restores 0x08000800 (X server driver functions rexCopyRect, rexDrawImage, rexValidateWindowPriv). Inferred from that pairing: drawing coordinate = loaded coordinate plus (x origin minus 0x800), so the pair puts the screen x of the run unchanged while keeping the engine coordinate at 4 or more; a model that applies the origin offset to the coordinates gets the right pixels, one that ignores XYWIN draws four pixels to the right. The ide test keeps 12 bits per half.
